To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We propose an extension to Convolutional Neural Nets (CNNs) for graph-structured data.

(1) we introduce a new type of convolutional neural network that works on graphs, which (2) achieves the accuracy of existing CNNs on images, (3) without any prior knowledge of the 2D regular image structure, (4) and that (5) obtains a significant improvement over existing graph-based methods on fMRI data.

we propose an extension of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and strided convolutions for graph structured data, that we apply this method to fMRI and achieve a significant gain in prediction accuracy, and that we achieve this gain while matching the performance of CNNs on image data, without using any prior about the regular structure of images.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following two problems: (i) How to define a convolution on a graph, and (ii) how to define an augmentation of a graph.
two questions: How to design a convolutional neural network that is applicable to graph-structured input? How to train this network?
the development of new methods and tools for data analysis and visualization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the method proposed here can be applied to any type of data, regardless of the underlying graph, and can be used as a drop-in replacement for existing CNNs.
CNNs can be extended to graph-structured input data and can be used for graph classification.
our method can be applied to any graph-structured data and is able to match the state of the art in accuracy, while not requiring prior assumptions about the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are the first ones to apply CNNs on graphs.
our method allows to use the same CNN architectures for both 2D and 3D data, with a single hyperparameter.

we have proposed a generalization of CNNs to graph-structured input data, that is applicable to both images and fMRI data, and that is able to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy without any prior about the 2D regularity of images.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CNNs can be extended to graph-structured inputs, without the need of a prior about the data regularity.
graph-based data can be processed by CNNs, and that the resulting networks are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches.
graph-structured data can be analyzed with CNNs without any prior about the graph structure, and that this approach can outperform state-of-the-art graph-based methods.
